What SEO Is Now: How Search Ranking Works Today

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 19 June 2026 · 7-minute read · Distribution

In short: Modern SEO rewards pages that answer the query better than the alternatives, are technically sound and are trusted by other sites; it punishes volume and tricks. Search engines now answer many queries directly, and Ahrefs found an AI Overview correlated with a 58% lower click-through rate for the top result by late 2025. AI assistants are a parallel channel, and both reward clear early answers and checkable claims. Payback is slow, often slower than plans assume, but every company should do the minimum.

Key points

  • Google names five ranking signals: the meaning of the query, relevance, quality, usability, and the searcher's context and settings.
  • Google also uses "aggregated and anonymized interaction data" and whether "other prominent websites link or refer to the content".
  • Pew found users clicked a result on 8% of Google visits with an AI summary, against 15% without one.
  • Mass-produced pages made to manipulate rankings or AI answers breach Google's scaled content abuse policy.
  • In Ahrefs' 2025 data, only about 6% of new English pages reached the top 10 within a year; the average number-one page was five years old.

Search engine optimisation is the practice of making a website more likely to appear when people search for what it offers. The name has survived twenty-five years. The practice underneath it has changed almost completely, and a great deal of advice still circulating describes a search engine that no longer exists.

How ranking works, in outline

A search engine crawls the web, reads pages, stores what it finds and, when someone searches, picks and orders the pages most likely to satisfy the query. Google's own description lists five "key Search signals": the meaning of the query, the relevance of content, the quality of content, its usability, and the searcher's context and settings, such as location and search history.

Two further statements on the same page matter. Google says "one of the factors used to determine quality is understanding if other prominent websites link or refer to the content". And it says "we also use aggregated and anonymized interaction data to assess whether search results are relevant to queries". In other words, the ordering considers what the page says, how usable it is, what other sites say about it, and how searchers have responded to it.

The engine's interest is the searcher's satisfaction. Everything that has changed in SEO is the engine getting better at measuring that and worse at being fooled.

What still matters

Content that answers the query better than the alternatives. Google defines "people-first content" as "content that's created primarily for people, and not to manipulate search engine rankings". Its self-assessment asks whether a page provides "original information, reporting, research, or analysis".

Technical health. Pages that load fast, render on phones, can be crawled and are not duplicated. Google says that when other signals are similar, more usable pages may rank higher.

Clear structure. Titles, headings and links that describe what is where.

Authority. Being linked to, cited and mentioned by sites the engine already trusts.

Demonstrable expertise. Named authors with real credentials, especially for financial and health topics. Google's guidance says "Your Money or Your Life" topics, which affect health, finances, safety or wellbeing, receive extra scrutiny, and that trust carries the most weight among its experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trust criteria.

Satisfying the intent. A searcher who wanted a comparison, given a sales page, leaves, and the engine notices.

What stopped mattering, or became harmful

Keyword density and exact-match repetition. Buying links. Spinning many thin pages around variations of a phrase. Tricks that show the engine something different from what users see. And publishing large volumes of generic content, now easier than ever with AI and more heavily penalised for the same reason.

Google's helpful content guidance lists warning signs, including "Are you using extensive automation to produce content on many topics?" Its July 2026 guide on AI features states that creating pages primarily "to manipulate rankings or generative AI responses in Google Search" violates its scaled content abuse policy. Independent evidence points the same way for AI answers: in the GEO study (KDD 2024), keyword stuffing lowered a source's visibility in generated answers by about 8%, while adding statistics and quotations raised it.

What changed most recently

Two things. The engines now answer many queries directly, with a summary at the top generated from pages they retrieve, and searchers increasingly do not click through. And AI assistants have become a parallel search channel with their own retrieval and citation behaviour.

The click evidence is consistent across independent and vendor sources:

StudySampleFinding
Pew Research Center, July 2025900 US adults, 68,879 searches, March 2025Result clicked on 8% of visits with an AI summary, 15% without; session ended on 26% against 16%
Ahrefs, February 2026 (vendor)300,000 keywords, December 2023 against December 2025AI Overview correlated with 58% lower click-through for the top result
Seer Interactive, November 2025 (agency)3,119 informational queries across 42 clientsOrganic CTR on AI Overview queries fell from 1.76% to 0.61%; cited brands had higher CTR than uncited ones

The direction matters more than any single figure. Seer's own numbers are internally inconsistent in places, and both vendor studies show correlation, not cause. But no credible study shows clicks rising on informational queries.

Both shifts reward the same things: pages that state a clear answer early, make specific checkable claims, are structured so a machine can extract them, and are corroborated by other trusted sources. Both punish content that exists to rank rather than to answer. Google says its AI features need "no additional requirements" beyond ordinary eligibility for Search. Our pieces on how AI answer engines choose sources and the LLM optimization checklist cover the mechanics.

Everything that has changed in SEO is the engine getting better at measuring searcher satisfaction and worse at being fooled.

What this means for a company deciding whether to invest

SEO has a long payback. Our working assumption has been six to twelve months before organic traffic covers the cost of the content. The evidence says to treat that as the fast case. Ahrefs' 2025 study of new pages found only about 6% of English pages reached the top 10 for any keyword within a year. The average page in position one was five years old, and 72.9% of top-10 pages were more than three years old. Pages that do break through can move fast: about 41% of those reaching the top 10 did so within a month. Most never do. Fewer clicks per ranking stretch the payback further.

For a company with short runway and no existing audience, that can be longer than it can afford, and it is fair to say so. Our piece on demand generation economics sets out how to compare a slow channel with faster ones.

The calculation changes when the company already has authority to build on, when the category's paid channels are closed to it, or when the content would be written anyway for sales, support or partners. In those cases, writing it once, properly, for search and AI citation together, is close to free distribution. Our guide to distribution when ad platforms restrict you covers the closed-channel case.

The honest minimum

Even a company that decides not to invest in SEO should do the minimum:

  1. A fast, crawlable site with accurate titles and descriptions.
  2. Business information that is consistent everywhere it appears.
  3. Structured data for the organisation.
  4. A handful of pages that answer the questions buyers actually search for, each with a named author where expertise matters.
  5. No technical mistakes that hide the site, including robots.txt rules that block search crawlers by accident.

In our experience that is about a week of work, and it is the difference between being findable and not. Payback is slow, so invest deliberately, but never skip the minimum.

lowob takeaways

  • The engine measures satisfaction. Meaning, relevance, quality, usability and context, plus links and interaction data.
  • Volume is now a liability. Mass-produced pages breach Google's scaled content abuse policy and do worse in AI answers.
  • Clicks are falling on informational queries. Plan for citation and for fewer visits per ranking.
  • Payback is slower than most plans. Treat six to twelve months as the fast case; most new pages never reach the top 10.

Common questions

What still matters for SEO in 2026?

Content that answers the query better than alternatives, technical health, clear structure, links and mentions from trusted sites, named authors with real expertise on finance and health topics, and matching what the searcher wanted.

How long does SEO take to pay off?

Plan on at least six to twelve months, and longer in competitive categories. Ahrefs found only about 6% of new English pages reached the top 10 within a year, though those that did often got there within a month.

Do AI Overviews reduce clicks to websites?

The evidence says yes for informational queries. Pew found result clicks fell from 15% to 8% of visits when a summary appeared, and Ahrefs measured a 58% lower click-through rate for the top result.

What is the minimum SEO every company should do?

A fast, crawlable site with accurate titles and descriptions, consistent business information, organisation structured data, a few pages answering what buyers search for, and no technical mistakes that hide the site.

Next Move

Open Search Console and list the ten queries with the most impressions and the fewest clicks. For each, check whether an AI summary appears and whether your page is cited in it, then rewrite the weakest page so its answer and evidence come first.
